cards.q: What two things are true of a reversible reaction at dynamic equilibrium?
cards.a: The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backward reaction, and the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.
cards.why: “Dynamic” because both reactions are still happening; nothing changes overall because they happen at the same rate.

cards.q: Why can dynamic equilibrium only be reached in a closed system?
cards.a: In an open system products (especially gases) can escape, so the backward reaction cannot keep pace and the reaction never settles.
cards.why: A closed system lets no substance in or out, so the forward and backward rates can become equal.

cards.q: True or false: at equilibrium the concentrations of reactants and products are equal.
cards.why: The equilibrium mixture can be mostly products, mostly reactants, or anything between; it is the rates that are equal.

cards.q: True or false: once a reaction reaches equilibrium, the reactions stop.
cards.a: False. Both the forward and backward reactions continue, at equal rates.
cards.why: This is why it is called a dynamic equilibrium.

cards.q: State Le Chatelier’s principle.
cards.a: If a factor affecting a system in equilibrium is changed, the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose the change.
cards.why: It predicts the direction of the shift; it does not say how far the position moves.

cards.q:
\(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}(aq) + SCN^{-}(aq) \rightleftharpoons [FeSCN]^{2+}(aq)}\)
The complex ion on the right is blood red. Predict and explain what you would see when more \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) ions are added.
cards.a: The solution becomes a deeper red.
marks: Adding \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) increases the concentration of a reactant.
The position of equilibrium shifts to the right to remove the added \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) (oppose the change).
More \(\mathrm{[FeSCN]^{2+}}\) forms, so the red colour deepens.

cards.q:
\(\mathrm{N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_{3}(g)}\)
Explain the effect of increasing the total pressure on the equilibrium yield of ammonia.
marks: There are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 moles of gas on the right.
Increasing the pressure shifts the position of equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas, to reduce the pressure.
So the equilibrium shifts to the right and more ammonia is formed.

cards.q: What is the effect of increasing the pressure on the position of the equilibrium \(\mathrm{H_{2}(g) + I_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)}\)?
cards.a: No effect on the position of equilibrium.
cards.why: There are 2 moles of gas on each side, so neither direction reduces the pressure. Both rates increase equally, so equilibrium is reached faster.

cards.q:
\(\mathrm{2SO_{2}(g) + O_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2SO_{3}(g)}\) \(\Delta H = -196\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
Explain the effect of increasing the temperature on the equilibrium yield of \(\mathrm{SO_{3}}\).
marks: The forward reaction is exothermic, so the backward reaction is endothermic.
Increasing the temperature shifts the position of equilibrium in the endothermic direction, to absorb the heat.
So the equilibrium shifts to the left and less \(\mathrm{SO_{3}}\) is formed.

cards.q:
\(\mathrm{[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}(aq) + 4Cl^{-}(aq) \rightleftharpoons [CoCl_{4}]^{2-}(aq) + 6H_{2}O(l)}\)
pink on the left, blue on the right. The solution turns blue when heated. Explain what this shows, and predict the effect of adding water.
cards.a: The forward reaction is endothermic. Adding water turns the solution pink.
marks: On heating, the position of equilibrium shifts to the right (more blue complex).
An increase in temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction, so the forward reaction is endothermic.
Adding water increases the concentration of a product, so the position of equilibrium shifts to the left.
More pink \(\mathrm{[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\) forms.

cards.q: What is the effect of a catalyst on a reaction at equilibrium?
cards.a: It has no effect on the position of equilibrium, but equilibrium is reached more quickly.
cards.why: A catalyst increases the rates of the forward and backward reactions by the same factor.

cards.q: True or false: adding a catalyst to the Haber process increases the equilibrium yield of ammonia.
cards.a: False. A catalyst does not change the yield at equilibrium; it only gets there faster.
cards.why: It speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally, so the position of equilibrium does not move.

cards.q: Ammonia for fertiliser is made by \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_{3}(g)}\), \(\Delta H = -92\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), at about 450 °C. Explain why this temperature is a compromise.
cards.a: A lower temperature gives a higher yield but too slow a rate.
marks: The forward reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature would give a higher equilibrium yield.
But at a low temperature the rate is too slow, so equilibrium would take too long to reach.
A moderate temperature gives an acceptable yield at an acceptable rate.

cards.q: The Haber process runs at about 200 atm. Explain why a higher pressure is not used, even though it would increase the yield of ammonia.
cards.a: Higher pressures cost too much to produce and are more dangerous.
marks: A higher pressure would increase both the yield and the rate.
But producing very high pressures needs a lot of energy for the compressors, which is expensive.
The plant would need thicker, stronger pipes and vessels, which cost more to build, and the risk of an explosion is greater.

cards.q: In the Contact process, \(\mathrm{2SO_{2}(g) + O_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2SO_{3}(g)}\), the equilibrium yield of \(\mathrm{SO_{3}}\) is already over 95% at 1 to 2 atm. Why is a high pressure not used?
cards.a: The yield is already very high, so the small gain from a high pressure does not justify the extra cost.
cards.why: Industry weighs yield, rate and cost together: here pressure would add cost for almost no benefit.

cards.q: Ethanol is made by \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4}(g) + H_{2}O(g) \rightleftharpoons C_{2}H_{5}OH(g)}\), \(\Delta H = -46\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), at about 300 °C and 6 to 7 MPa with a phosphoric acid catalyst. Why is a high yield per pass not essential?
cards.a: Unreacted ethene is separated and recycled, so almost all of it is eventually converted, even though only a small fraction reacts on each pass.
cards.why: Recycling allows a compromise temperature and pressure that give a good rate at reasonable cost.

cards.q: True or false: industry always uses the conditions that give the highest equilibrium yield.
cards.a: False. Conditions are a compromise between yield, rate and cost (including energy and safety).
cards.why: A high yield is of little use if equilibrium takes days to reach, or the plant is too expensive to build and run.

cards.q: Write the expression for \(K_{\text{c}}\) for the general reaction \(\mathrm{aA + bB \rightleftharpoons cC + dD}\).
cards.why: Products over reactants, each concentration (in mol dm⁻³, at equilibrium) raised to the power of its coefficient in the equation.

cards.q: Write the expression for \(K_{\text{c}}\) for \(\mathrm{H_{2}(g) + I_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)}\), and give its units.
cards.why: The units cancel: \(\frac{( \text{mol dm}^{-3})^{2}}{( \text{mol dm}^{-3})( \text{mol dm}^{-3})}\).

cards.q: Write the expression for \(K_{\text{c}}\) for \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_{3}(g)}\) and deduce its units.
cards.why: Cancel the concentration terms first, then flip any left on the bottom by making the powers negative.

cards.q: Write the expression for \(K_{\text{c}}\) for the esterification \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH(l) + C_{2}H_{5}OH(l) \rightleftharpoons CH_{3}COOC_{2}H_{5}(l) + H_{2}O(l)}\).
cards.why: All four substances are in the same liquid phase (a homogeneous system), so water is included in the expression.

cards.q: At equilibrium, \([\mathrm{H_{2}}] = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\), \([\mathrm{I_{2}}] = 3.0 \times 10^{-3}\) and \([\mathrm{HI}] = 1.74 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\). Calculate \(K_{\text{c}}\) for \(\mathrm{H_{2}(g) + I_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)}\).
cards.why: Give the answer to the same number of significant figures as the least precise data (here 2).

cards.q: 1.00 mol of ethanoic acid and 1.00 mol of ethanol were mixed with an acid catalyst. At equilibrium the mixture contained 0.667 mol of ethyl ethanoate. Calculate \(K_{\text{c}}\).
steps: At equilibrium: ester \(= 0.667\) mol and water \(= 0.667\) mol.
cards.why: Use the equation’s mole ratio to find every equilibrium amount before substituting.

cards.q: 0.400 mol of \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\) and 0.200 mol of \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\) were sealed in a 2.00 \(\text{dm}^{3}\) vessel. At equilibrium there was 0.300 mol of \(\mathrm{SO_{3}}\). Calculate \(K_{\text{c}}\) for \(\mathrm{2SO_{2}(g) + O_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2SO_{3}(g)}\).
cards.why: 0.300 mol of \(\mathrm{SO_{3}}\) forms from 0.300 mol of \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\) and only 0.150 mol of \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\) (1 : 2 ratio).

cards.q: For \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO_{2}(g)}\), \(K_{\text{c}} = 4.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) at a certain temperature. At equilibrium \([\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}}] = 0.100\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\). Calculate \([\mathrm{NO_{2}}]\).
cards.why: Rearrange the expression first; remember to take the square root at the end.

cards.q: For \(\mathrm{H_{2}(g) + I_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)}\), \(K_{\text{c}} = 50\) at a certain temperature. What is \(K_{\text{c}}\) for \(\mathrm{2HI(g) \rightleftharpoons H_{2}(g) + I_{2}(g)}\) at the same temperature?
cards.why: Writing the equation the other way round turns the expression upside down, so the new constant is the reciprocal.

cards.q: What does the size of \(K_{\text{c}}\) tell you about the position of equilibrium?
cards.a:
A large \(K_{\text{c}}\) (much greater than 1): the equilibrium lies to the right (mostly products).
A small \(K_{\text{c}}\) (much less than 1): it lies to the left (mostly reactants).
cards.why: Products are on the top of the expression, so more products gives a bigger value.

cards.q: Which single factor changes the value of an equilibrium constant?
cards.why: Changing concentration or pressure, or adding a catalyst, can move the position of equilibrium or speed it up, but leaves the constant unchanged.

cards.q: How does increasing the temperature affect the value of \(K_{\text{c}}\) for (a) an exothermic reaction and (b) an endothermic reaction?
cards.why: Higher temperature favours the endothermic direction, so the yield of products (the top of the expression) falls for an exothermic reaction and rises for an endothermic one.

cards.q: For an exothermic reaction, explain in terms of \(K_{\text{c}}\) why increasing the temperature moves the position of equilibrium to the left.
cards.a: The temperature rise lowers \(K_{\text{c}}\); the mixture then reacts backwards until the concentrations fit the new, smaller value.
marks: Increasing the temperature decreases the value of \(K_{\text{c}}\) for an exothermic reaction.
Immediately after the change, the ratio \(\frac{[\text{products}]}{[\text{reactants}]}\) is greater than the new \(K_{\text{c}}\).
So products react to form reactants until the ratio equals the new \(K_{\text{c}}\): the equilibrium shifts to the left.

cards.q: More reactant is added to a mixture at equilibrium at constant temperature. Explain, in terms of \(K_{\text{c}}\), why more product forms.
cards.a: \(K_{\text{c}}\) is unchanged, so the system reacts forwards until the ratio of concentrations equals \(K_{\text{c}}\) again.
marks: \(K_{\text{c}}\) depends only on temperature, so its value does not change.
Adding reactant increases the bottom of the expression, so the ratio \(\frac{[\text{products}]}{[\text{reactants}]}\) is now less than \(K_{\text{c}}\).
Reactants form products until the ratio equals \(K_{\text{c}}\) again, so the position of equilibrium shifts to the right.

cards.q: True or false: adding more of a reactant increases the value of \(K_{\text{c}}\), because more product forms.
cards.a: False. \(K_{\text{c}}\) stays the same; the position of equilibrium shifts.
cards.why: More product forms, but the reactant concentration is also higher, so the ratio returns to the same value of the constant.

cards.q: What is the difference between a homogeneous and a heterogeneous equilibrium?
cards.a:
Homogeneous: all the species are in the same phase.
Heterogeneous: the species are in more than one phase, such as solids with gases or with a solution.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{H_{2}(g) + I_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)}\) is homogeneous; \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s) \rightleftharpoons CaO(s) + CO_{2}(g)}\) is heterogeneous.

cards.q: Write the expression for \(K_{\text{c}}\), with units, for \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}(aq) + Fe^{2+}(aq) \rightleftharpoons Ag(s) + Fe^{3+}(aq)}\).
cards.why: Solids are left out of the expression for a heterogeneous equilibrium: their concentration is constant.

cards.q: For \(\mathrm{Fe_{3}O_{4}(s) + 4H_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 3Fe(s) + 4H_{2}O(g)}\), the equilibrium concentrations are \([\mathrm{H_{2}O}] = 0.020\) and \([\mathrm{H_{2}}] = 0.030\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\). Calculate \(K_{\text{c}}\).
cards.why: The units cancel because the powers on the top and bottom are equal.

cards.q: True or false: \(K_{\text{c}}\) for \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s) \rightleftharpoons CaO(s) + CO_{2}(g)}\) is \(\dfrac{[\mathrm{CaO}][\mathrm{CO_{2}}]}{[\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}]}\).
cards.why: The concentration of a pure solid does not change, so it is included in the value of the constant.

cards.q: Define mole fraction and partial pressure for a gas in a mixture.
cards.a:
Mole fraction: \(x_{\mathrm{A}} = \dfrac{\text{moles of A}}{\text{total moles of gas}}\)
Partial pressure: \(p_{\mathrm{A}} = x_{\mathrm{A}} \times\) total pressure.
cards.why: The partial pressure is the pressure gas A would exert if it alone filled the container. The partial pressures add up to the total pressure.

cards.q: An equilibrium mixture contains 2.0 mol \(\mathrm{N_{2}}\), 6.0 mol \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\) and 2.0 mol \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) at a total pressure of 200 kPa. Calculate the partial pressure of \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\).
cards.why: Check: the partial pressures (40, 120 and 40 kPa) add up to the total, 200 kPa.

cards.q: Write the expression for \(K_{\text{p}}\) for \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO_{2}(g)}\).
cards.why: Same pattern as Kc, but with equilibrium partial pressures instead of concentrations.

cards.q: Write the expression for \(K_{\text{p}}\) for \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_{3}(g)}\), and give its units when pressures are in kPa.
cards.why: \(\dfrac{\text{kPa}^{2}}{\text{kPa} \times \text{kPa}^{3}} = \text{kPa}^{-2}\)

cards.q: Write the expression for \(K_{\text{p}}\) for \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_{3}(g)}\), and give its units when partial pressures are in atm.
cards.why: \(\dfrac{\text{atm}^{2}}{\text{atm} \times \text{atm}^{3}} = \text{atm}^{-2}\)

cards.q: An equilibrium mixture of 0.60 mol \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}}\) and 0.80 mol \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\) has a total pressure of 100 kPa. Calculate \(K_{\text{p}}\) for \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO_{2}(g)}\).
cards.why: Units: \(\frac{\text{kPa}^{2}}{\text{kPa}} = \text{kPa}\).

cards.q: 2.00 mol \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\) and 1.00 mol \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\) reach equilibrium at a total pressure of 150 kPa; 80.0% of the \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\) has reacted. Calculate \(K_{\text{p}}\) for \(\mathrm{2SO_{2}(g) + O_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2SO_{3}(g)}\).
cards.why: Find all the equilibrium moles from the equation’s ratios first; the total moles change because the numbers of gas moles differ on each side.

cards.q: At equilibrium, the partial pressures are \(p_{\mathrm{NH_{3}}} = 30\), \(p_{\mathrm{N_{2}}} = 40\) and \(p_{\mathrm{H_{2}}} = 130\ \text{atm}\). Calculate \(K_{\text{p}}\) for \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_{3}(g)}\).
cards.why: Cube the hydrogen pressure before multiplying: a very common slip.

cards.q: 1.00 mol of \(\mathrm{PCl_{5}}\) is heated; at equilibrium 40.0% has dissociated and the total pressure is 2.00 atm. Calculate \(K_{\text{p}}\) for \(\mathrm{PCl_{5}(g) \rightleftharpoons PCl_{3}(g) + Cl_{2}(g)}\).
cards.why: Units: \(\frac{\text{atm} \times \text{atm}}{\text{atm}} = \text{atm}\).

cards.q: Write the expression for \(K_{\text{p}}\) for \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s) \rightleftharpoons CaO(s) + CO_{2}(g)}\), with units.
cards.why: Only gases appear in a Kp expression; the solids are left out.

cards.q: For \(\mathrm{C(s) + H_{2}O(g) \rightleftharpoons CO(g) + H_{2}(g)}\), the equilibrium partial pressures are \(p_{\mathrm{H_{2}O}} = 0.40\ \text{atm}\) and \(p_{\mathrm{CO}} = p_{\mathrm{H_{2}}} = 0.80\ \text{atm}\). Calculate \(K_{\text{p}}\).
cards.why: Units: \(\frac{\text{atm} \times \text{atm}}{\text{atm}} = \text{atm}\).

cards.q: \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO_{2}(g)}\) is endothermic in the forward direction. What happens to \(K_{\text{p}}\), and to the position of equilibrium, when the temperature is raised?
cards.a: \(K_{\text{p}}\) increases, and the position of equilibrium shifts to the right (more brown \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\)).
cards.why: A temperature rise favours the endothermic direction, which increases the equilibrium constant for an endothermic reaction.

cards.q: For \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO_{2}(g)}\), the total pressure is doubled at constant temperature. Explain why \(K_{\text{p}}\) does not change but the position of equilibrium moves to the left.
cards.a: \(K_{\text{p}}\) depends only on temperature; doubling the pressure makes the ratio of partial pressures too big, so some \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\) reacts.
marks: \(K_{\text{p}}\) depends only on temperature, so it is unchanged.
Doubling the total pressure doubles each partial pressure, so \(\frac{(p_{\mathrm{NO_{2}}})^{2}}{p_{\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}}}}\) doubles and is now greater than \(K_{\text{p}}\).
\(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\) forms \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}}\) (fewer gas moles) until the ratio equals \(K_{\text{p}}\) again: the position shifts left.

cards.q: True or false: increasing the total pressure increases \(K_{\text{p}}\) for \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_{3}(g)}\), because the yield of ammonia goes up.
cards.a: False. \(K_{\text{p}}\) is unchanged; only the position of equilibrium moves.
cards.why: An equilibrium constant changes only with temperature. The mole fractions adjust so that the expression returns to the same value.

cards.q: What is the effect of a catalyst on the value of \(K_{\text{p}}\), and on the time taken to reach equilibrium?
cards.a: No effect on \(K_{\text{p}}\); equilibrium is reached more quickly.
cards.why: A catalyst increases the rates of the forward and backward reactions equally, so it cannot change the equilibrium mixture.

cards.q: True or false: if \(K_{\text{p}}\) for a reaction decreases when the temperature is raised, the forward reaction is endothermic.
cards.why: Raising the temperature favours the endothermic (here backward) direction, so less product forms and the constant falls.

cards.q: Outline how \(K_{\text{c}}\) for the formation of ethyl ethanoate from ethanoic acid and ethanol can be found by experiment.
cards.a: Mix known amounts with a little acid catalyst, seal and leave to reach equilibrium, then titrate the acid present with standard sodium hydroxide.
steps: Mix known masses (moles) of ethanoic acid, ethanol and a small known volume of dilute hydrochloric acid catalyst; seal and leave for about a week at constant temperature.
Titrate the mixture with standard sodium hydroxide solution, using phenolphthalein indicator.
Subtract the moles of acid catalyst (found by titrating the same volume of catalyst alone) to get the moles of ethanoic acid at equilibrium.
Use the equation to find the other equilibrium amounts; the volume cancels in \(K_{\text{c}}\).
cards.why: Water in the catalyst solution must be counted in the initial amount of water.
